read.sections.0.heading.source: Extra food helped the first cities grow
read.sections.0.heading.back: Surplus food helped the first cities grow

read.sections.0.text.note: Real places in their usual Thai names: เมืองอูรุก (Uruk), แม่น้ำหวงเหอ (Yellow River; some books write แม่น้ำฮวงโห or แม่น้ำเหลือง). The checker warns that the Latin names Uruk and others do not appear: the brief asks for usual Thai names for real places, so this is on purpose.
read.sections.0.text.source: More than 5,000 years ago, some farming towns grew into the first cities. One of the earliest was Uruk, in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq. Other early cities grew beside the Nile in Egypt and the Indus River in South Asia. Some grew in the Yellow River valley in China. Later, cities also grew in Mexico, Central America and West Africa. Every city needed a food surplus. With extra food, thousands of people could eat without farming. Then many people could specialise in one kind of work. They became builders, potters, traders or priests. In Banwa, extra grain lets potters, builders and record keepers each do one main job.
read.sections.0.text.back: More than 5,000 years ago, some farming communities grew into the first cities. One of the very first was the city of Uruk in Mesopotamia, which is in the country of Iraq today. Other early cities grew along the Nile in Egypt and along the Indus in South Asia. Some cities grew in the Yellow River valley in China. Later, cities also appeared in Mexico, Central America and West Africa. Every city needed surplus food. With leftover food, thousands of people could eat without farming. So many people could specialise; they became builders, potters, traders or priests. In Banwa, leftover grain let potters, builders and record-keepers each do a different main job.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: More than 5,000 years ago, the first cities began. Uruk, in what is now Iraq, was one of the first. Other cities grew by big rivers in Egypt, South Asia and China. Later, cities grew in the Americas and West Africa. A city needs a surplus, or extra food. Then many people do not need to farm. They can specialise. Some build, and some trade. In Banwa, extra grain lets people do one main job.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: More than 5,000 years ago, the first cities began. Uruk was one of the first cities. Uruk is in today's Iraq. Other cities were by big rivers, in Egypt, South Asia and China. Later, there were cities in the Americas and in West Africa. A city needs surplus food, which is food left over. Then many people don't have to farm. They can specialise. Some build, some trade. In Banwa there is leftover grain, so people can do just one main job.

read.sections.1.heading.source: States had rulers, laws and taxes
read.sections.1.heading.back: States have rulers, laws and taxes

read.sections.1.text.note: King Hammurabi written กษัตริย์ฮัมมูราบี, the usual Thai school spelling (ประมวลกฎหมายฮัมมูราบี), rather than Latin letters: a real historical person, read aloud by a Thai voice. "temples" is วิหาร (ancient temples); check it does not read as a Buddhist วิหาร only.
read.sections.1.text.source: Many cities became part of a state. A state is a group of people in one area who are led by one government. Rulers and officials made choices for everyone and settled arguments. They also made laws, which are rules that everyone must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on a tall black stone. States collected taxes too, and people often paid in grain, animals or work. In Egypt, farmers gave part of their harvest to the ruler. Taxes paid for canals, walls, storehouses and temples. In Banwa, leaders organise a canal and make rules about the water.
read.sections.1.text.back: Many cities became part of a state. A state is a group of people in one area led by the same government. Rulers and officials make decisions for everyone and settle quarrels. They also make laws, which are rules everyone must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on a tall black stone pillar. States also collected taxes, and people often paid in grain, animals or labour. In Egypt, farmers had to give part of their harvest to the ruler. Taxes were used to build canals, walls, granaries and temples. In Banwa, leaders organise digging canals and set rules about water use.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Many cities became part of a state. A state is an area with one government. Its leaders make laws. A law is a rule that all people must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi put his laws on a big stone. People also paid a tax, often in grain or work. The tax paid for walls and canals. In Banwa, the leaders plan a canal and make water rules.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Many cities became part of a state. A state is an area with one government. The state's leaders make laws. Laws are rules everyone must follow. In Babylon there was a king named Hammurabi. He had laws written on a big stone. People also had to pay taxes, often in grain or labour. Taxes were used to build walls and canals. In Banwa, leaders plan digging canals and set rules about water.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Writing helped, but power was not shared equally
read.sections.2.heading.back: Writing helped, but power was not shared equally

read.sections.2.text.source: To collect taxes and share out food, officials needed to keep track of a lot. So some early states began to keep a record in writing. In Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain and animals. Egypt, China and the Maya of Central America also made their own writing. The Indus cities had signs too, but nobody can read them yet. Working together, a city could build things that one family could not. But power was not shared equally. Rulers, officials and rich families often controlled land, grain and water. Some laws protected people, but others helped the powerful more.
read.sections.2.text.back: Officials had to keep track of many things to collect taxes and share out food. So some early states began keeping written records. In Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain and animals. Egypt, China and the Maya in Central America also invented their own writing. The cities of the Indus valley had signs too, but no one can read them yet. By working together, a city builds things one family couldn't build. But power was not shared equally. Rulers, officials and rich families often controlled land, grain and water. Some laws protected people, but some helped those with more power.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Leaders needed to count lots of grain. So some states started to keep a record in writing. In what is now Iraq, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain. Egypt, China and the Maya made writing too. No one can read the Indus signs yet. In a city, people can build big things together. But power is not shared fairly. Rulers and rich families often have more land and grain. Some laws help the rich more.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Leaders had to count a lot of grain. So some states began writing records. In the land that is now Iraq, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain. Egypt, China and the Maya had writing too. Cities by the Indus River had signs too, but no one can read them yet. In cities, people could work together to build big things. But power was not shared fairly. Rulers and rich people often had more land and grain. Some laws helped rich people more.

write.example.source: Banwa began to change when its farms grew extra grain for several years. This meant that people could build a big store for the grain. Some people could stop farming and work as potters, builders or traders. Next, the leaders planned a canal and made rules about the water. Records helped because the record keeper could count the grain and the tax. Some people gained more power because they had more land and grain than other families.
write.example.back: Banwa began to change when the fields grew more grain than needed for many years in a row. This meant people could build a big granary to store grain. Some people stopped farming and became potters, builders or traders. Later, the leaders planned digging canals and set rules about water. Records helped because the record-keeper could count grain and taxes. Some people gained more power because they had more land and grain than other families.

watch.summary.source: This video tells the story of ancient Egypt, one of the world's early states. The Nile River runs through a dry desert. Each year, the river flooded and left rich soil on its banks. Farmers used this soil to grow large amounts of grain. The surplus fed many people who did other work, such as builders, craftspeople and scribes, who wrote records. The Nile was also like a road. Boats carried food, stone and other goods up and down the river. Egypt was ruled by kings called pharaohs, with many officials to help them. They collected taxes, planned work and kept records. This let Egypt build huge projects. But power was not shared equally. Egypt is only one example. Other early cities and states grew in different ways.
watch.summary.back: This video tells about ancient Egypt, one of the world's early states. The Nile flows through dry desert. Every year the river floods and leaves fertile soil along its banks. Farmers used this soil to grow lots of grain. Surplus food fed many people doing other work, such as builders, craftspeople and scribes, who were people who wrote records. The Nile was also like a road: boats carried food, stone and other goods up and down the river. Egypt was ruled by a king called a pharaoh, helped by many officials. They collected taxes, planned work and kept records. This let Egypt build huge structures. But power was not shared equally. Egypt is just one example. Other early cities and states grew in different ways.

educatorNotes.1.source: Present large states as one way of organising people, not as more 'civilised' or better. The Indus cities, for example, show no clear palaces or kings, and many smaller societies had their own laws, trade and knowledge.
educatorNotes.1.back: Present large states as one way of organising people, not as something more "civilised" or better. For example, Indus valley cities have no clear evidence of palaces or kings, and many small societies had their own laws, trade and knowledge.

educatorNotes.2.source: The video is one case study (Egypt). Remind learners that other early states grew in different ways. Lesson 12 looks at how modern cities grow; keep the two lessons separate.
